grammar.title: 4B: Ability and possibility - can, could, be able to
grammar.explanation:
**can** is a modal verb for ability and possibility. It has only one form, but we also use it with future meaning.

For past ability and possibility, we use **could**. It is the past of **can** and also works in conditional sentences.

For every other tense or form — the perfect, the infinitive, the gerund — there is no form of **can**, so we use **be able to** + infinitive.

We sometimes use **be able to** in the present and past too, when we want to sound more formal.

In the negative past, both **couldn't** and **wasn't able to** are possible.
examples: I *can* book a round trip online in five minutes. (present ability)
Our daughter *could* swim across the pool when she was six. (past ability)
She has *been able to* travel alone since her first excursion. (present perfect — no form of can exists)
I would love *to be able to* take a cruise next summer. (infinitive — after 'to')
He enjoys *being able to* choose an aisle seat every time. (gerund — after 'enjoy')
After the long transfer, we *weren't able to* find our stopover hotel. (past negative)

practice.q: Can we use 'can' after 'to'? Fix this sentence: 'I want to can speak French.'
practice.a: No. Say: 'I want to be able to speak French.'

practice.q: Talk about last year (past ability): 'You ___ drive to the coast?'
practice.a: 'Could you drive to the coast?' — or the more formal 'Were you able to drive to the coast?' Both are correct.

practice.q: Which is correct: 'She will can join us' or 'She will be able to join us'?
practice.a: 'She will be able to join us.' Can has no future form.
